name: Scythians and Saka
summary: Iranian-speaking nomadic horse peoples of the Eurasian steppe, from the Black Sea (Scythians) to Central Asia (Saka). They were famed horse archers, and their gold work and burial mounds survive.

knownFor.label: Scythian gold
knownFor.note: Animal-style gold work such as the Tolstaya Mogila pectoral.

knownFor.label: Horse archers
knownFor.note: Riders who shot short composite bows from the saddle.

knownFor.label: Kurgans
knownFor.note: Large burial mounds for chiefs, with horses and treasures.

location.value: The Pontic Steppe north of the Black Sea (modern Ukraine and southern Russia), after migrating from Central Asia.

terrain.value: Open grassland with river valleys; mountains in the east.

climate.value: The Pontic Steppe was wet and damp in the 1st millennium BCE, so grass grew in abundance for their herds.

resources.value: Rich grassland for large herds of horses and cattle; grain from settled forest-steppe peoples, taken as tribute.

urbanisation.value: Mostly nomadic at first; later many settled, and Kamianka became the capital in the late 5th century BCE.

migration.value: Migrated from Central Asia to the Pontic Steppe in the 9th–8th centuries BCE.

economicBase.value: Nomadic herding of horses, cattle and sheep; grain tribute from settled peoples and trade with the Greeks.

tradeRoutes.value: Sold grain, slaves, fish, furs and cattle to Greek colonies on the Black Sea in return for luxury goods such as wine.

wealth.value: Aristocrats were buried with lavish grave goods, including gold jewellery and fine Greek-made vessels.

moneyAndTax.value: Used coins for trade with the Greeks but never in their own domestic market.

inequality.value: A ruling aristocracy above commoners, serfs and slaves; slaves tilled the land and tended cattle.

governmentType.value: A monarchy: the king of all the Scythians was chief of the dominant tribe, the Royal Scythians.

keyRulers.value: King Idanthyrsus (about 530–510 BCE). King Ateas, killed fighting Philip II of Macedon in 339 BCE.

succession.value: Hereditary royal clans, as described by Herodotus.

institutions.value: Clan groups formed the basis of community and politics; a custom of blood brotherhood existed.

armyAndTech.value: Mounted archers with powerful composite bows; aristocrats wore scale armour of bone, bronze or iron.

majorWars.value: Raided West Asia (7th century BCE); attacked by Darius I of Persia (513 BCE); defeated by Philip II of Macedon (339 BCE).

territoryChange.value: Conquered by the Sarmatians in the 3rd–2nd centuries BCE; the Scythian settlements in Crimea were destroyed around 200 CE.

alliancesRivals.value: Traded with the Greeks and served them as mercenary archers; fought the Persians and Macedonians; close ties with the Thracians.

inventions.value: Saddle cloths, trousers for riding, and the composite bow were used widely by steppe peoples like them.

scienceEducation.value: Had no written language; known from Greek writers such as Herodotus and from archaeology.

openness.value: Their art absorbed Greek, West Asian and Thracian influences.

communicationTransport.value: Nomads lived in wagons and felt tents and moved with their herds.

religion.value: Soothsayers used cannabis for trance and divination; goddesses such as Artimpasa were influenced by Mesopotamian religion.

languageWriting.value: Eastern Iranic languages; a western branch survived as the language of the Alans and modern Ossetian.

artsArchitecture.value: The “Animal Style” art, showing animals in set poses; skilled goldsmithing and bronze-casting.

socialStructure.value: Patriarchal and clan-based, led by a warrior aristocracy; women warriors appeared after Sauromatian immigration.

sharedIdentity.value: Shared nomadic culture across a huge area rather than one nation.

dailyLife.value: Lived in wagons and felt tents; ate meat from their herds and drank mare’s milk, also made into cheese.

ideasReligions.value: Greek art influenced Scythian goldwork; steppe styles spread into Europe and China.

colonisation.value: Saka groups founded kingdoms in north-west India and Afghanistan (Indo-Scythians).

riseSignals.value: Mastery of horse riding and archery.

peakPeriod.value: A period of prosperity in the 4th century BCE.

declineSignals.value: Climate change, overgrazed pastures, military setbacks and the arrival of the Sarmatians in the early 3rd century BCE.

outcome.value: Overwhelmed by the Goths by the 3rd century CE and absorbed by other peoples during the Migration Period.

sources.value: Wikipedia: Scythians; Wikipedia: Saka; Herodotus, Histories, Book 4; Cunliffe, The Scythians (2019).

overallCertainty.value: Known mostly from Greek writers and archaeology; many details are uncertain.
